extracted.intended_audience: aspiring novelists, students of literature, and literary critics
extracted.subtask_description: Practical and critical guidance for writing and judging English-language novels: identifies principal 'aspects' (Story, People, Plot, Fantasy, Prophecy, Pattern and Rhythm) and related techniques (point of view, tone, detail, characterization).

rubrics_metrics.name: The Story
rubrics_metrics.description: The story is 'a narrative of events arranged in their time sequence' and is the fundamental, backbone aspect of the novel; its primary literary tool is suspense—the reader's desire to know 'what happens next' (Scheherazade example).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make the audience wonder what will happen next; use chronological arrangement to sustain curiosity. Forster warns that story is a low/atavistic form (the backbone/tapeworm) and that excellence cannot rest on story alone: story keeps readers awake but without other qualities it may be unadmirable. Examples: Scheherazade's interrupted sentences; caution that mere story-telling, however effective, is not the highest aim.

rubrics_metrics.name: People
rubrics_metrics.description: The persons (characters) in a novel — how they are conceived, drawn and made to live on the page — is a central aspect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how convincingly characters are presented and how they interact with story and plot. Forster treats 'People' as a chief aspect and discusses techniques such as point of view, dialogue, and the balance between character-consistency and surprise. Look for whether the novel's human material is allowed to breathe (avoid stiff external forms that kill humanity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Flat characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters constructed around a single idea or quality that remain essentially the same throughout a book.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flat characters are useful (comic types, minor figures) and are easier to sustain; they can be memorable and function as motifs. Forster notes they are 'constructed' and reproducible. Beware over-reliance: too many flat figures can make a work superficial, but the flat character is an established and legitimate device.

rubrics_metrics.name: Round characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Complex characters capable of surprising the reader in a convincing way; they resemble real people and can develop or reveal unsuspected aspects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim to create characters who can act unexpectedly yet remain consistent in motive; roundness is a mark of psychological depth. Forster privileges round characters for their likeness to life and their centrality to novelistic art; they resist simple classification.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Plot
rubrics_metrics.description: Plot is distinct from story: it is not just sequence but events arranged so that one thing leads to another (causal connection), producing inevitability or a sense of meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use causation to give events weight and purpose; avoid contrived devices that force causality. Forster contrasts plot with mere chronological story and discusses how plotting produces a different reader experience — purpose, destiny, or moral consequence — while warning that over-systematic plotting can become an external exercise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fantasy
rubrics_metrics.description: A novelist's employment of imagination: starting from little objects or incidents, taking a 'flutter' from them and expanding into imaginative meditation (Sterne, Virginia Woolf as exemplars).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use small details as launching points for imaginative digression; cultivate a tone of deliberate bewilderment when appropriate. Forster shows that fantasy can combine humour and sense of life's muddle; technique matters (execution differs between writers even when medium is similar).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prophecy
rubrics_metrics.description: The novelist's faculty for apprehending or announcing truths about man/society — not necessarily literal forecasting but the power to 'prophesy' in moral or social perception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether a novel has a prophetic dimension: insights that transcend its immediate subject-matter and reveal wider human or social truths. Forster treats 'Prophecy' as one of the aspects to consider, meaning the work's capacity to illuminate or warn rather than its accuracy in predicting future events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pattern
rubrics_metrics.description: External formal arrangement or pattern imposed on a work (symmetry, rigid design); an artistic form that can create 'beauty' but may 'externalize the atmosphere' and cut the novel off from life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patterns can produce beauty but risk tyranny: they may shut doors on life and reduce characters to exercises. Forster argues that pattern is more defensible in drama than in the novel because the novel's material is too human and messy for strict external form. Use pattern sparingly and avoid letting it dominate human truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhythm
rubrics_metrics.description: Internal binding device achieved by repetition plus variation (small-scale leitmotifs) and — possibly — a larger-scale rhythmic unity analogous to musical structure; rhythm can stitch a chaotic novel together from the inside.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ recurring phrases, images, musical 'little phrases' (Proust's Vinteuil motif) and variation to create internal cohesion and beauty without rigid external form. Forster distinguishes 'easy' rhythm (repetition/variation) from the elusive larger rhythm analogous to a symphony; rhythm should wax and wane to refresh the reader rather than harden into predictable symbolism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Point of view
rubrics_metrics.description: The narrator's vantage point and technique (who tells the story and how): choice of point of view shapes perception, tone, and reader alignment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be attentive to historical and technical differences in point-of-view usage (Forster notes use of 'he said'/'she said' varies through centuries). Select a point of view that suits the desired intimacy, objectivity, or irony; misuse can distort character and mislead readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone and authorial voice
rubrics_metrics.description: The novelist's tone (humorous, aloof, ardent, visualizing, etc.) and the 'novelist's touch' — the manner in which prose invites or resists the reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match tone to subject and be wary of an intrusive authorial presence ('the face of the author draws rather too near to that of the reader'). Forster compares humorists (Wells, Dickens) and aloof modernists (Woolf) to show how tone shapes perceived taste and scope. Cultivate the appropriate degree of intimacy and restraint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of detail and visualization (cataloguing)
rubrics_metrics.description: The skillful cataloguing and visualization of particulars (objects, gestures, settings) to produce atmosphere, humour, or social judgement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Details can create comic or social effects (Forster's comparisons of funeral descriptions); but excessive or mechanical cataloguing can produce scratchy prose or expose the author unduly. Use detail to illuminate character and scene, not to parade knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humanity / Affection as the final test
rubrics_metrics.description: Forster's axiom: 'The final test of a novel will be our affection for it' — the novel is 'sogged with humanity' and its power depends on evoking human sympathy and attachment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the novel gains the reader's affection; beware of exorcising humanity in pursuit of form (the novel wilts without it). Sentimentality must be kept from dominating critical judgment, but absence of human warmth is fatal to many novels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sensitiveness (novel's mirror)
rubrics_metrics.description: The novel's success depends on its sensitiveness — its capacity to perceive and render human feeling — more than on topical subject-matter or historical situation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize the novel's internal sensitiveness and perception over merely choosing 'important' subjects; a novel's art is not determined by its topicality but by the way its author makes the mirror of fiction sensitive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and scope of 'novel'
rubrics_metrics.description: A practical working definition used by Forster: 'a fiction in prose of a certain extent' — he suggests an extent 'not less than 50,000 words' and construes 'English' as written in English (not limited by geography).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the 50,000-word threshold as a pragmatic delimiter for the genre in this critical context; be explicit about language and scope when applying the aspects. This is descriptive rather than evaluative, but it sets the subtask's boundaries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of rigid pseudo-scholarly classification
rubrics_metrics.description: A methodological injunction for critics: avoid classifying novels by crude chronological, topical, or formulaic categories ('the literature of weather', 'the novel of passion after 1847', etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics and writers should read books thoroughly rather than subsume them under portable 'tendencies' or taxonomies. Forster calls such classification the mark of the pseudo-scholar and warns it misleads judgment; evaluation should be grounded in close reading and attention to the aspects above.
